title: From a household brief to a workable cooking routine
intro: A managed private chef service in Dubai should make the arrangement easier to understand from the first conversation. You bring the details of your home, preferences and schedule; myCHEF helps translate them into a proposed chef match, menu and service plan. The value is in connecting those decisions so nothing important is left to assumption. This expanded guide follows the practical work behind the introduction, explains what to prepare for the first visit and shows how feedback can keep the arrangement useful as your routine changes.

sections.title: What happens between your enquiry and the first meal?
paragraphs: The brief needs enough detail to assess availability and suitability before a menu is promised. Your location, intended start date, meal coverage and essential dietary requirements are the foundation. Kitchen equipment and grocery responsibilities then help define the work.

Once a suitable arrangement is proposed, you can ask questions about the chef, timing and scope. Confirm the written details before service begins. That sequence gives you a clear decision at each stage and helps the professional arrive with a useful understanding of the home rather than discovering every requirement on the day.

sections.title: Send a brief that makes the first proposal useful
paragraphs: A useful enquiry can be short and still contain the essentials. Include your Dubai location, preferred date or start date, number of people, the meals you need and any essential dietary requirements. Add whether the service is a recurring household arrangement or a one-off occasion, because those lead to different menus, staffing and pricing discussions.

Then describe what a successful result would feel like. Perhaps you want dinner ready when you arrive home, a fridge organised for several busy days or a celebration where you can stay with your guests. This helps the team recommend a suitable format instead of making you choose from options that do not address your main priority.

If you have a budget in mind, share it with the scope. That creates a practical starting point for discussing the number of courses, frequency or staffing. An enquiry begins a conversation; the final menu, availability, responsibilities and price are confirmed in the written booking details.

sections.title: Look for a chef whose strengths fit the brief
paragraphs: A chef who excels at an elaborate tasting menu may not be the best match for a household that wants simple daily meals and careful batch preparation. Start with the work you actually need: particular cuisines, family cooking, confident service for guests or a regular routine with multiple meals. Relevant experience matters more than a list of impressive-sounding dishes.

Discuss the proposed chef's approach to your kitchen and schedule. How would the menu fit the available hours? Which dishes work well for later meals? What information would they need before the first visit? These practical questions make an introduction more useful than a general conversation about favourite food.

myCHEF considers the brief alongside availability when recommending a match. Profiles can help you understand cooking interests and service styles, but the proposed arrangement still needs confirmation. If you would like a paid trial or tasting, agree the purpose, menu and price first so you know exactly what you will be assessing.

sections.title: Agree how ingredients reach your kitchen
paragraphs: There are two practical starting points for groceries: have the agreed ingredients ready before the visit, or discuss shopping as part of the service. Either way, the menu needs a clear list. Quantities, preferred brands and acceptable alternatives help avoid delays when an ingredient is unavailable or a household staple has run out.

Keep the service fee and grocery spending easy to understand. Your written proposal should explain who shops, whether shopping time is included in the booked hours and how ingredient costs are handled. If you want a premium cut, specialist imported item or a particular organic product, include that in the brief so it can be priced and sourced appropriately.

It also helps to identify what is already in the kitchen. A quick check of oils, seasonings, rice and other staples can reduce duplicate purchases. For ongoing cooking, agree how the chef should flag low stock and ask before making substitutions that materially change the meal or its cost.

sections.title: Plan arrival time around preparation, not just mealtime
paragraphs: The time you want to eat is different from the time the chef needs to arrive. Ingredients may need preparation, several dishes may need different cooking stages and the table may need attention before guests sit down. Give the team your preferred meal time and ask for an arrival schedule that reflects the agreed menu.

For recurring visits, consider when the kitchen is busiest. Breakfast routines, school departures, deliveries and household staff schedules can all affect access to the workspace. A sensible start time allows the chef to work comfortably while keeping disruption to your household low. If you work from home, mention rooms or periods that need to stay quiet.

Also confirm when the service is expected to finish and what happens if plans run late. Additional tasks or extended service may require more time and an extra charge under the agreed terms. Raising these possibilities before the day is easier than trying to negotiate them while a meal is already underway.

sections.title: Make the first visit a useful foundation
paragraphs: For the first visit, choose a menu that gives the chef a realistic picture of your household. Include food you know well enough to give useful feedback on, rather than making every dish unfamiliar. Keep the priorities clear: which meal matters most, what should be prepared for later and what time the kitchen needs to be ready.

Allow a short introduction to the space. Show the chef the appliances, utensils, storage areas and any items that need special care. Confirm the grocery arrangements and clarify which household member should answer questions if you are unavailable. This helps prevent small uncertainties from interrupting the cooking repeatedly.

At the end, review the practical handover as well as the food. Know which dishes are ready to eat, which need finishing and what instructions apply to them. Then share feedback on portions, taste and timing. The first visit is an opportunity to make the next one more precise, comfortable and useful for everyone involved.

sections.title: Make feedback specific enough to act on
paragraphs: The easiest way to improve an ongoing service is to describe the result you want. Instead of saying a meal was not right, explain whether it was too rich, too spicy, too large or served later than expected. A specific observation gives the chef a useful direction for the next menu and makes it easier to check whether the adjustment worked.

Tell us what you enjoyed as well. A dish you would happily eat again, a helpful way of organising the fridge or a cooking day that fitted your schedule can become part of the regular plan. Consistency is built from these details, not simply from repeating a menu without checking how it is being used.

For a service concern, contact myCHEF promptly with the relevant facts. The next step may be a menu change, a clearer brief, a revised schedule or discussion of a different available match. Any remedy depends on the circumstances and the booking terms; the starting point is a clear conversation.

cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
